newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Political war looms after S.Korea's Kim apologises.
newsitem.headline: Political war looms after S.Korea's Kim apologises.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam, fighting to save his administration, apologised for election spending abuses on Friday but defiantly refused to offer any details of his finances.
Instead, Kim challenged opponents who accuse him of overspending in the 1992 presidential polls to help clean up the system. And he suggested they were just as guilty.

His remarks, part contrite and part combative, were broadcast live on television. Far from defusing a crisis in a presidential election year, they threatened to bring about open war between the opposition and the head of state, who is already wounded by a corruption scandal that has led to the arrest of his son.
A solemn Kim noted that his 1992 campaign spending had "become a political issue of late".
"Before all else, each of us in political life, including myself, must reflect humbly and publicly repent for past wrongs," he said.

He said spending abuses were a legacy of a corrupt past, adding: "You can very well imagine that nearly five years later it is impossible to account in detail for the total amount spent under such hectic circumstances".
Opposition parties allege that Kim's 1992 election was partly bankrolled by the scandal-ridden Hanbo Group and his disgraced predecessor, Roh Tae-woo.
The leader of the National Congress for New Politics, Kim Dae-jung, blasted the speech as "pompous and confrontational" and vowed a head-on fight with the president.
He again alleged that Kim Young-sam took 300 billion won ($336 million) from Roh and 60 billion won from Hanbo to fund a campaign in which spending for each candidate was capped at 36.7 billion won.
"I have evidence and witnesses," he told reporters.

Roh is serving a 17-year jail sentence for corruption and other crimes. Hanbo is at the centre of a loans-for-kickbacks scandal that has led to the arrest of Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, and several of his top aides.

"We cannot tolerate this any longer. We have decided to fight the president directly," said Kim Dae-jung, a candidate in presidential elections in December. He said he would demand an independent probe by parliament.

The president's opponents are on dangerous ground since leaders of all parties are widely assumed to have overspent. However Kim Young-sam is especially vulnerable since he was swept to power pledging to sever the corrupt collusion between politicians and big business.
Ordinary South Koreans appeared disappointed at an apology that fell far short of expectations.

The president must step down at the end of his single term next February, but scandals have paralysed his administration as it grapples with an economic downturn and seeks to implement crucial financial reform.
"The speech didn't say anything important. I felt deeply deceived," said Kim Young-jun, an elderly man watching the broadcast on a screen at Seoul's main railway station.

Kim Young-sam called on all parties to help draft new legislation on election funding to end the system of money-politics. Among other reforms, he called for a ban on mass rallies and private political organisations.
If "myopic partisan interests" scuttled the effort, he warned he would have to take an unspecified "grave decision".
"I urge you to stop the exhausting political disputes on election funds involved in the last presidential election that are causing the country to drift," he said.
It was Kim's second apology over the so-called "Hanbogate" scandal. He first expressed remorse in a televised speech to the nation in February.

"The investigation of the Hanbo affair has clearly shown us how deeply the collusion between politicians and businessmen in our country has taken root in society. It has plainly shown the ugly state of our politics," he said.
